astra.text:
Yeah. I think the first thing is, is your baseline strong enough? Because, as we saw in ConvNeXt, you can have a very familiar architecture, but if you train it with an older recipe, you can get a very different conclusion about how good that architecture is. So I would first want to make sure that the baseline also benefits from these, these improvements in training and design.

And then, when you introduce a new component, you want to control the other things as much as possible. The data, the training compute, the other architectural details. If you change all of them together, you can say you have a better model, but it's harder to say that this particular inductive bias is why it's better, right?

But it's also tricky because the same training recipe may not be equally good for two different architectures. So I think you need to give both of them some opportunity to be tuned. Otherwise, you might just be measuring which architecture works better with the recipe you already chose.

And, ideally, I would want to see whether the improvement holds at different scales, on different tasks. That is also the difficult part for academia, because doing these comparisons carefully can be very expensive. So I wouldn't say there is one perfect set of controls. But at least the claim should match what you actually demonstrated. Showing an improvement in one setting is useful; understanding why that improvement happens requires more work.

sol.text:
Yeah, that’s a very good question. I think the first rule is that you need a really strong baseline, and you need to give the baseline the same amount of care as the new method. The data, augmentation, optimizer, training length, regularization, parameter count, FLOPs—all of these should be controlled as much as possible. And importantly, the amount of hyperparameter tuning should also be comparable. Very often, people spend months tuning the new architecture and then compare it with a baseline using a recipe copied from an older paper. Then it’s hard to know what actually caused the improvement.

But there is a subtlety: different architectures may prefer different recipes. So I would want to see both comparisons. One is under exactly the same recipe, which isolates the architectural change. The other is with each model reasonably tuned, which tells us the best practical performance each one can achieve.

And then I would require the result to hold across scales—not just one small model on one benchmark. Ideally, you test multiple model sizes, multiple datasets or tasks, and also report actual training and inference efficiency, not only FLOPs. You should include careful ablations, because components interact, and some estimate of variance across runs if the gain is small. If an inductive bias is real, I would expect it to give a consistent advantage in the regime where the theory says it should help, rather than a tiny improvement at one operating point. Otherwise, I would be very cautious about claiming that the inductive bias itself is responsible.

r002.rationale: It explicitly requires comparable hyperparameter tuning and criticizes tuning the new architecture more extensively than the baseline.

r003.rationale: It recommends multiple datasets or tasks, but does not clearly require that those datasets be reasonably scaled.

opus.text:
Yeah, that's, that's a good question. I think about this a lot, and, and yes, I do tell my students some version of this.

So the first one, the most basic one, is compute matching. Like you have to compare at, at matched FLOPs and parameters, and, and also please report actual wall-clock throughput, because a lot of, a lot of designs look great on paper in terms of FLOPs but they're, they're slow on real hardware. So, so that's, that's kind of table stakes.

But the, the one I care about the most, and the one that's violated the most often, is the, the training recipe has to be identical, and the, the hyperparameter tuning budget has to be equal for the baseline. what usually happens is people, people spend three months tuning their new method, and then they, they copy the baseline number from a paper from 2016 that was trained with a completely different, augmentation and optimizer and schedule. And, and then they report a two point gain. And, and in ConvNeXt, I mean, that, that was literally the finding, right? Like a big chunk of the, the gap we were told was about self-attention was, was just recipe. The baseline was, was under-trained. So, so I would say if, if you can't show me that your baseline got the same, the same care that your method got, I, I don't, I don't really believe the number.

then, the, the third one is, show me more than one point. Like a single model at a single scale, on a single dataset, that's, that's an anecdote. I want to see a, a trend across at least two or three model sizes and, and ideally two or three data scales. Because inductive bias specifically, this is the thing, right? inductive bias is a, is a substitute for data. so almost every inductive bias helps in the small data, small model regime, and then a lot of them just, just wash out, or, or even become harmful once you scale up. So if, if you only show me the small scale point, you haven't really told me whether this matters or whether you've just, you've just found something that, that data would have taught the model anyway.

And then, some smaller things. Multiple seeds and, and some sense of the variance, because a lot of these, these 0.2, 0.3 differences on ImageNet are, are just noise. And, and please add your component to a, a strong modern baseline rather than a weak old one, because things that help a, a badly tuned network often do nothing once the network is, is already healthy.

and then the last thing is, is more about honesty than about controls. we, we in academia often genuinely cannot run the, the large scale experiment. that's, that's just the reality. So, so then I think the right thing is to scope the claim. Say, at this scale, on this data, with this recipe, I observe this. rather than, like, this inductive bias is, is fundamentally better. that's, that's a much more, more defensible paper, and honestly, I, I think it's a more useful one, because the, the failure mode of the field is not that people run small experiments. It's that people, people write universal conclusions from them. Yeah.

grok.text:
Yeah. Yeah, I, I think that’s exactly the thesis, that the field very often confounds architecture with recipe. People change the model, they also change how they train it, and then they attribute the whole gain to the inductive bias.

So if I were setting rules, for students, for papers, the first control is the recipe has to be held fixed. Same data, same number of epochs, same optimizer, same augmentation, same regularization. If you cannot keep them identical, then at least apply the new recipe to the old architecture as well and show that comparison. That’s, that’s the ConvNeXt lesson, right? A lot of the apparent transformer advantage was from the training setup, not from self-attention itself.

Second, match the budget. Similar parameters, similar FLOPs, and if you care about practice, similar throughput. You cannot claim a new inductive bias is better if the model is just bigger, or trained longer, or trained on more data.

Third, isolate the claim. If you want to say this new bias matters, change that one thing, and show the ablation. Don’t change the stem, the stage ratio, the activation, the normalization, and a new attention variant all at once, and then say, this bias is what did it. We saw in ConvNeXt that a lot of small details add up, and nothing single-handedly explains the gap.

And I would also want it at more than one scale. Sometimes a story looks great at a small model and disappears when you go bigger, or the other way around. And if you can, more than one task. ImageNet alone can be misleading. Transfer, detection, segmentation, or, if it’s language, more than one downstream eval, that gives me much more confidence it’s not just overfitting to one benchmark.

I think if you do all of that, and you still see a consistent gap, then you can start to say, okay, maybe this inductive bias actually matters. Otherwise I would be very skeptical. Yeah.

gemini.text:
Yeah, that's a very good question. 

First, I think the most important thing is that you have to strictly control the training recipe. A lot of times, what happens in architecture papers is people propose a new architecture with a new inductive bias, but they also use a completely modernized training recipe—better augmentations, different optimizers, longer training schedules—and then compare it against an older baseline that was trained with an outdated setup. So rule number one is you have to give the baseline the exact same modern training recipe, or modernize the baseline first, so you're actually comparing architectures and not recipes.

Second, you need very careful step-by-step ablations. As we saw in our ConvNeXt work, it's often not the core mechanism or the new inductive bias that brings the improvement, but rather the compounding effect of many small design details—like where you place activations, reducing normalization layers, or how you connect the layers. So before claiming that a specific inductive bias is the source of the gain, you have to isolate it and show that the advantage doesn't just come from these small, orthogonal design tweaks.

And finally, you have to evaluate along the efficiency and performance trade-off curve—whether that's compute, FLOPs, parameters, or latency. Because you can always change an architecture to add capacity or compute in subtle ways, but what really matters is whether this new inductive bias pushes the Pareto frontier forward. Without controlling for the recipe, the small details, and the efficiency budget, it's very easy to confound a recipe or tuning advantage with an architectural breakthrough.

r001.rationale: The response discusses efficiency and performance trade-offs but does not recommend demonstrating the architecture change at state-of-the-art scale such as roughly 7B or 30B parameters.

r002.rationale: It requires applying the same modern training recipe to the baseline, but does not explicitly require tuning hyperparameters for both the proposed architecture and baseline before comparison.

r003.rationale: The response does not require evaluation on multiple reasonably scaled datasets; it only discusses controlling recipes, ablations, and efficiency budgets.

kimi.text:
Okay. Yeah, I, I actually think about this a lot, and I do, I do discuss these, these exact rules with my students. So, the first and most important rule, I would say, is you have to modernize the baseline. Don't compare your new architecture against the, the original ResNet, or the original ViT with its, its old training recipe. Take the strongest existing model, train it with the best recipe you, you can find, and then make your change on top of that. Otherwise, you can't, you can't really attribute the gain to your new inductive bias, right? It might just be the, the recipe stuff, the, the training epochs, the augmentation, all these things.

Second, control for everything else. The same data, the same number of epochs, the same compute budget, roughly the same number of parameters and FLOPs. And also, tune both models to a, to a comparable degree. Like if, if you, tune your own model with a, a huge hyperparameter search, but you tune the baseline only lightly, that's, that's just not a fair comparison.

Third, I would require showing the, the trend across scales, not, not just one single point. Because many claimed advantages, they look really promising at, at small scale and then they, they just wash out when you scale up. So show me the, the performance versus compute curve at multiple sizes. If the inductive bias truly matters, the gap should persist, or, or hopefully even grow as, as you scale.

And, yeah, fourth, measure the thing you actually claim. If, if you claim your inductive bias gives you better data efficiency, then show the, the data scaling curve. If you claim better long, long-context behavior, then evaluate long context directly. Don't use, like, a, a single accuracy number on one benchmark as the evidence for, for everything.

And, and also, ablate one component at a time, like, like what we did in, in the ConvNeXt paper, so people can see which pieces actually, contribute, and which pieces are, are just along for the ride. Because oftentimes the, the headline mechanism contributes less than the, the accompanying small details.

And finally, report efficiency honestly, like wall-clock time, latency, memory, throughput, not just, just FLOPs, because FLOPs can be, can be pretty misleading, right? Some operations have low FLOPs but are, are slow in practice.

So if a paper does all of these things and the, and the advantage is still there, persistently, across scales, then I would be convinced that, okay, this inductive bias, it, it genuinely matters. But honestly, very few, very few papers pass all of these tests. it's, it's hard, especially with the, the compute constraints in, in academia. But I think this is the, the standard we should, we should aim for. Yeah.

fable.text:
Yeah, that's, that's a good question. So I think the, the first rule, and, and this is what I tell my students, is that the baseline has to be treated as, as well as your own method. Like, this is, this sounds obvious, but, most of the time when people show, a new inductive bias, a new architecture is better, the baseline is, is trained with, an old recipe, maybe from three years ago, and the new method is trained with, the newest recipe with, with all the augmentation, with all the, the regularizations, with, with the learning rate that was tuned for the new method. And then the gap you see is really the recipe gap, not the, not the architecture gap. So, so we would say, you need to use the same training recipe, same data, same augmentation, same optimizer, same, schedule for, for both, and ideally you tune the hyperparameters for, for the baseline with the same amount of effort. And, and if the baseline gets better after you do that, you have to report it. Like, don't, don't just report the number from, from the original paper.

The second thing is you need to, control the, the cost. So, when you compare, compare, compare at the same FLOPs or same number of parameters or, or actually more importantly, same, throughput, same, latency on the actual hardware, because, a lot of the, the inductive biases that look, look good on paper, they are, they, they are just adding capacity in a, in a hidden way. Right? Like you add some, some module and it, it uses more compute and then, of course it's better. So, so that's, that's not really the inductive bias, that's the, that's the compute.

And then the third one, I would say, is scale, and, and, and diversity of, of tasks. So, a lot of inductive biases, they help, when, when data is small. That's, that's kind of the, the definition, right? Inductive bias is what, what you put in when, when you don't have enough data to learn it. So if you only show it on, on, on a small dataset or one benchmark, I, I'm not, I'm not convinced. You need to show that the, the gain stays there or at least doesn't, doesn't, doesn't go away when you, when you scale the data and scale the model. Because, in, in many, many cases, it's, it's the opposite. The, the gap just shrinks and then, and then it's, it's gone, and, and the, the more general architecture wins, because the, the data can, can just learn that bias itself. So, so ideally you show, like, a few points on the scaling curve, not just, not just one point.

And, and maybe, the last one, which is more, like a, a mindset thing, is, ablate, ablate one thing at a time.
